---
title: "From Raw Prices to a Clean Panel"
subtitle: "Download, parse, and turn prices into returns"
---



Every market example in this course runs on one small table: daily **returns**
for 14 stocks.  This page shows where that table comes from and how it's built —
the download, the parse, and the one transformation (prices → log-returns) that
turns raw quotes into something we can do statistics on.

---

## 1 · The Source and the Basket

The prices come from the public **S&P 500 "5yr"** file in the
[`plotly/datasets`](https://github.com/plotly/datasets) repository: ~500 names of
daily close prices from **2013-02-11 to 2018-02-07**.  We keep a curated
**14-stock basket** spanning five sectors — chosen so the dependence lessons are
visible to the naked eye: five banks that crash together, two mega-cap tech names,
energy, and defensive utilities/staples that march to a different drum.

::: {#tbl-basket .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
meta = datasets.load_basket_meta()
print(meta.to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why These 14?

The **sector** column is the story.  Banks (JPM, BAC, C, WFC, GS) share a risk
factor and move almost as one; utilities (DUK, SO) and staples (PG, KO) are
defensive and barely co-move with the banks.  That spread of behaviour is exactly
what makes correlation, co-crashes, and tail dependence *legible* later.
:::

## 2 · The Pipeline

The download script does four things: fetch the long-format price file, pivot it
to a wide *price panel* (one column per ticker), drop days with any missing
quote, and convert prices to **log-returns**.  The committed script is
[`scripts/download_market_data.py`](../../scripts/download_market_data.py); its
core is just:

```python
# scripts/download_market_data.py (excerpt — runs once, needs network)
df   = pd.read_csv(SP500_5YR_URL, parse_dates=["date"])      # long format
wide = df.pivot(index="date", columns="Name", values="close")
prices = wide[BASKET].dropna(how="any")                      # price panel
rets   = np.log(prices / prices.shift(1)).dropna(how="any")  # log-returns
rets.to_csv("data/processed/returns_basket.csv")
```

We don't re-download at page-render time (CI has no network); the result is
committed as `data/processed/returns_basket.csv` and loaded with
`datasets.load_returns()`.

::: {#f262858a .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
R = datasets.load_returns()
print(f"panel shape : {R.shape[0]} trading days x {R.shape[1]} assets")
print(f"date range  : {R.index.min().date()} -> {R.index.max().date()}")
print()
print(R.iloc[:3, :6].round(4).to_string())   # a corner of the table
```

## 3 · Why Log-Returns?

A **return** answers "how much did one dollar grow today?"  We use the *log*
return $r_t = \log(P_t / P_{t-1})$ rather than the simple percentage change for
two reasons: log-returns **add up over time** (a week's return is the sum of its
days), and they're roughly symmetric, which keeps the statistics well-behaved.

Because they add up, we can run the transformation **backward** to recover a price
path from returns — a cumulative sum inside an exponential.  We don't ship prices,
so we reconstruct an illustrative path here (starting every name at 100) purely to
*see* what the returns encode:

::: {#cell-fig-price-paths .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
meta = datasets.load_basket_meta().set_index("ticker")
prices = 100 * np.exp(R.cumsum())            # P_t = 100 * exp(sum of log-returns)

sector_color = {
    "Banks": plotting.CRASH, "Tech": plotting.COOL, "Energy": "#b08968",
    "Utilities": plotting.PALETTE["green"], "Staples": plotting.PALETTE["purple"],
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.6))
seen = set()
for t in prices.columns:
    sec = meta.loc[t, "sector"]
    ax.plot(prices.index, prices[t], color=sector_color[sec], lw=1.2, alpha=0.8,
            label=sec if sec not in seen else None)
    seen.add(sec)
ax.set_ylabel("price (indexed to 100)"); ax.set_xlabel("date")
ax.set_title("Five years, 14 names, coloured by sector", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, ncol=5, loc="upper left")
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Reconstructed price paths (each name indexed to 100 at the start), coloured by sector. Banks move as a tight bundle; utilities and staples drift more calmly. This is the cumulative story the daily returns table encodes.](01-downloading-and-parsing_files/figure-html/fig-price-paths-output-1.png){#fig-price-paths width=1065 height=537}
:::
:::


And the round-trip confirms the formula: re-deriving log-returns from the
reconstructed prices reproduces the original table exactly.

::: {#b9898a8f .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
back = np.log(prices / prices.shift(1)).dropna(how="any")
print(f"max |reconstructed return - original| = {np.abs(back - R.loc[back.index]).to_numpy().max():.2e}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
max |reconstructed return - original| = 4.41e-16
```
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
## The Takeaway
One table, two views: the **returns** are what we do statistics on (stationary,
additive); the **prices** are the cumulative story they tell.  Everything in the
market chapters starts from `datasets.load_returns()`.
:::
